title: Prayer Niche (Mihrab)

image.credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of Katharine Holden Thayer (1962.23)
image.license: Public domain. Released under the Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access program

altText: A tall, arched niche made of ceramic mosaic, with bands of calligraphy and decorative patterns. It is a mihrab, the focal point of a mosque's interior.

source.verifiedBy: Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access API record (title, culture, date, medium, credit line, description, did-you-know, CC0 status, image URL)

context: A ceramic mosaic prayer niche (mihrab) in the Cleveland Museum of Art, made in Iran, Isfahan, in the style of the Safavid period (1501–1722). The museum dates it "c. 1500s or mid-1900s": the calligraphy and design suggest a date around 1500, but testing of the tiles in 2001 pointed to 1941–1961.

descriptions.k: This is a prayer niche called a mihrab. It is shaped like an arch and made from many small tiles. Look for the curved top. Look for the patterns and the writing. Which pattern do you like best?
descriptions.g12: A mihrab is a special niche in a mosque that shows which way to face for prayer. This one is made of many pieces of colored tile, set together like a puzzle. Look for the arch and for the writing and patterns. Where do you see a pattern that repeats?
descriptions.g35: This mihrab, or prayer niche, is made of ceramic mosaic and comes from Iran, from Isfahan, in the style of the Safavid period. A mihrab is the focal point of a mosque's interior and always points toward Mecca. Look at the arch, the calligraphy and the patterns. How do the tiles work together to make one design?
descriptions.g68: This ceramic mosaic mihrab was made in Iran, in Isfahan, in the style of the Safavid period (1501–1722). The museum explains that a mihrab is the focal point of a mosque, set in the wall that faces Mecca. Its date is uncertain: calligraphy and design suggest about 1500, but tile testing points to the 1900s. How do the arch, calligraphy and patterns work together, and why might a date be hard to settle?
descriptions.g910: This Prayer Niche (Mihrab) is a ceramic mosaic from Isfahan, Iran, in the style of the Safavid period. The Cleveland Museum of Art notes that calligraphy and design suggest a date around 1500, while thermoluminescence testing in 2001 dated the tiles to 1941–1961, with further examination underway. How does a work made in a historical style raise questions about authenticity, and how do the form and decoration of a mihrab communicate its function?
descriptions.g1112: This mihrab, a ceramic mosaic in the style of Safavid Iran (1501–1722), is dated by the museum "c. 1500s or mid-1900s." Its calligraphy and design suggest around 1500, but thermoluminescence testing of the tiles in 2001 indicated 1941–1961, and examination continues. How does the object challenge the line between an original and a work in an earlier style, and what do its function and decoration tell us about how sacred art is made and valued? Use evidence from the object and the record.

teacherNote.context: A ceramic mosaic prayer niche (mihrab) in the Cleveland Museum of Art, made in Iran, Isfahan, in the style of the Safavid period (1501–1722). The museum gives its date as "c. 1500s or mid-1900s."
directions: Have students create a paper mosaic arch from small cut shapes, repeating a pattern across the design.
Discuss what a niche or marker for direction does in a building, and invite students to share special places in their own communities respectfully.
Ask older students to discuss how scientific testing and style evidence can both help date an object, and why the museum gives a range.
